summary: Zeni-X is a smart agriculture system by Team Mesopotamia from Iraq. A miniature farm model uses an Arduino controller with soil-moisture and temperature/humidity sensors, water tanks, an irrigation pump and a solar panel. A live web dashboard shows the farm's status (soil moisture, soil pH, water levels, irrigation status, air temperature and humidity, sunlight and rainfall) with color-coded states and instant alerts. We compare the sensor readings with NASA POWER climate data for Najaf, Iraq, to verify them and support better irrigation decisions
details:
The project is the design and development of an integrated smart agriculture system made up of 14 interconnected systems. It aims to address a wide range of challenges facing the agricultural sector by employing Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, smart sensors, electronic systems, advanced software solutions and artificial intelligence (AI).

The core idea is a qualitative shift in traditional agricultural systems: turning automated systems that execute predefined commands into smart systems that can collect and analyze data, predict future changes, assess environmental conditions and make the right decisions proactively.

The system does not stop at automating farm operations; it aims to build an integrated farming environment that understands its surroundings, interacts with them and manages its resources efficiently based on data, analysis and prediction. The project combines artificial intelligence with application programming interfaces (APIs), giving priority to data sources from the U.S. space agency NASA and drawing on its Earth-observation, climate and environmental data to support analysis and agricultural decision-making.

This integration brings together readings from local sensors inside the farm and external environmental data, to build a more complete picture of the conditions that affect agricultural production.

💡 Example

For example, the system analyzes the likelihood of rain in the coming period. If the available data indicate rain is likely within the next hour, the system can compare this with the soil moisture level and the plants’ needs, then decide to postpone or adjust irrigation — avoiding repeated watering and overuse of water, and reducing the risk of soil salinization and degradation, which benefits plant health and crop quality.The project combines artificial intelligence with application programming interfaces (APIs), giving priority to data sources from the U.S. space agency NASA and drawing on its Earth-observation, climate and environmental data to support analysis and agricultural decision-making.
